Nothing was taken from Peng & Wu's original article; all text shipped here is the study's own S1 File, hence text_source=study_materials. (2) LANGUAGE: English, so no `language` column and no `_translated` columns are emitted. The S1 File questionnaire is printed in English throughout, the S2 workbook's AIC-CCS column headers are English item wording, and the paper names Chinese only for the sixteen follow-up interviews ('the interviews were conducted in Chinese, transcribed, and then translated into English') -- i.e. it distinguishes the two modes and attributes Chinese to the interviews alone. No Chinese-language questionnaire exists anywhere in the deposit or the supplements. Noting for the record that metadata/tags.csv carries Primary Language 'chi' for this table, which this extraction does not corroborate; the tag describes the sample (130 Chinese students in Ireland), not the instrument. (3) MAPPING, derivation pattern 1 (code IS the source column name): data/yang_2025_intercultural.py reads the 'Intercultural Contact' sheet and melts the literal columns FSM1..FSM3, FICA1..FICA6 with no rename and no positional step. mapping_basis is paper_explicit rather than data_labels because those column headers are bare codes carrying no wording -- the words come from S1 File, which prints the block code ('FSM', 'FICA') above a numbered list, so code prefix -> block is a label match and the within-block index -> line (1)(2)(3) is the questionnaire's own printed enumeration. Route 9: all 45 item x response-level counts computed from the raw S2 workbook match the live table exactly (FSM1 21/20/27/36/26, FSM3 30/28/26/20/26, FICA4 18/25/23/38/26, ...; 0 of 45 mismatched), and no two of the nine columns share a frequency vector, so any permutation of codes against workbook columns would have shown up. That rules out a processing-script permutation and confirms the 1-5 integers are the workbook's own values unrecoded. Route 3: the workbook's own 'FSM' and 'FICA' composite columns reproduce as the means of FSM1..3 and FICA1..6 to 0.0000 and 0.0033 (2 d.p. rounding in the stored composite) over all 130 rows, confirming block membership. NOT ESTABLISHED: which numbered questionnaire line within a block belongs to which index. The paper publishes no per-item statistic for this scale at all -- Table 9 is dimension-level Spearman correlations (FSM r=0.387, FICA r=0.412 with IC) -- and the live per-item means span only 2.877-3.223 on near-uniform distributions, so no statistical route can separate the texts within a block. Always=5. Basis: the questionnaire prints them left-to-right in that order under every item; the workbook stores 1-5 integers only; and the paper reads a higher score as more contact ('The FSM dimension correlates positively with IC (r = 0.387, p < 0.01), indicating that greater engagement...'), which fixes the direction. Route 9 shows the integers were not recoded between workbook and IRW, but it cannot itself fix the direction, because the workbook holds no labels. The Methods section states 'Sections II and III used a 5-point Likert scale, from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree)', but the S1 File questionnaire prints neither of those anchor sets for either section: Part II (AIC-CCS) is '(A) very low (B) low (C) average (D) high (E) very high' and Part III (this table) is 'Never Rarely Sometimes Often Always', which is also the only reading consistent with Part III's own instruction to answer 'based on the frequencies of your engaging in'. The questionnaire is the study's own instrument and is the better authority on what respondents saw, so its anchors ship; carried in public_note. Live items are exactly FSM1-3 and FICA1-6, resp 1-5, n=130 each, which is Part III of the questionnaire and matches the dictionary description ('Foreign Social Media + Foreign Intercultural Communication Activity contact scale (9 items 1-5 Likert) N=130'). (9) RIGHTS: no block, and no reserved right locatable. The wording shipped is the study's own questionnaire, published in a CC BY 4.0 PLOS ONE article's supporting information. The CSV is written and the gate passed; an unchanged retry would produce the identical file. The one open item, within-block item order, is a determinate gap rather than an access failure: the paper publishes no per-item statistic and the response distributions are too flat to discriminate, so only Peng & Wu's original item numbering or new material from the authors could upgrade PARTIAL to VERIFIED.
public_note: The item wording, instructions and response anchors are transcribed verbatim from the study's own questionnaire (S1 File of the CC BY article), including its typos -- item FICA5 reads 'lving in a homestay familiy abroad' as printed. Two things are worth knowing. First, the anchors shipped here are Never / Rarely / Sometimes / Often / Always, which is what the questionnaire prints above every item of this scale and what its instruction to answer 'based on the frequencies of your engaging in' implies; the paper's Methods section instead describes Sections II and III as running '1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree)', which matches neither section's printed anchors, so a reader comparing the two will find a discrepancy the questionnaire settles. Second, the workbook's column headers are bare codes (FSM1, FICA1, ...) and the questionnaire numbers its lines under the block headings 'Foreign Social Media (FSM)' and 'Foreign Intercultural Communication Activity (FICA)', so the block each item belongs to is certain but the order of the three FSM texts among themselves, and of the six FICA texts among themselves, follows that printed numbering and could not be checked against the data: the paper reports no per-item statistics and the nine item means span only 2.88 to 3.22. What was checked: all 45 item-by-response-level counts in the deposited workbook match the live table exactly, so no code was permuted in processing and the 1-5 integers are the source's own.
